segments.text: Why are neighbors pointing security cameras at a 170-acre mountain bike park,
then reporting visitors to the county prosecutor who wants the contact info of everyone there?
This is Panhandle Bike Ranch.
It's a mountain bike park in Sagal, Idaho,
owned by Scott and Jennifer Kalbach.
Their family loves mountain biking and wanted to share
this experience with the community.
So in 2023, after owning property up here for a decade,
they purchased 170 acres for a passion project.
The Kalbachs knew they'd need a permit,
So even hired a land use consultant beforehand.
That April, Bonner County first approved their conditional use permit to run as a recreational facility.
But it had tight restrictions.
By this point, word had gotten out and some neighbors opposed it.
So they appealed the decision and the call box did too, asking for things like more riders allowed and days open.
Once again, the permit got approved as well as the requested changes.
And if the community wanted to appeal, they'd have to do so in court.
By December, the county made it official.
The final plan detailed things like trails, parking, and bathrooms, and they'd open the following summer.
So the call box invested their life savings, about $2.5 million, into the ranch.
Gravity Logic, the team behind Whistler's Bike Park, even contracted the job, and they hired local labor to build the 10 trails.
Then in June 2025, only 10 days before opening, a judge revoked the permit.
You see, those negative neighbors did take the matter to court, saying it's basically a resort and they shouldn't have to sit and listen.
Apparently, the county failed to properly document why it approved the bike park.
This reversed the permit.
And it should have been an easy fix.
The county just needed a document what the judge asked for, but they refused.
Apparently, commissioners wanted a new hearing, and planning staff suggested they operate based on donations.
That way, the bike ranch wouldn't need a permit.
So the call box pivoted to form a nonprofit.
They also asked the county to recognize the bike ranch as a park, a definition they now fit.
But some people still didn't like this and formed a very vocal opposition group.
And then things escalated.
People on both sides put up and stole signs.
One neighbor allegedly fired guns into his berm 150 feet from the beginner trail.
And another neighbor used his backhoe to dig trenches in the road shortly after the call box fixed it.
Again, allegedly.
Then last fall, the county denied the park designation, giving them no option to appeal.
So the call box filed a lawsuit in court while continuing to build out the ranch.
Until this spring.
The county posted a stop work order as the case went before a judge, who agreed.
Now only people with a close personal relationship could use the park,
but the call box felt this was too vague, especially since violating the order could mean jail time.
I attended one of these hearings where the judge said having a gate means it's not a park.
So for now, the ruling stands.
And since neighbors like this have multiple cameras pointed at the property,
one woman emailed photos to eight people at the county,
with the prosecutor now demanding the names, contact info, and relationship of everyone there.
So would opponents prefer the bike park get sold to developers with an army of lawyers who
can rezone the land into a housing development?
